newsitem.title: BELGIUM: U.S.-French row holding up NATO plans to reform.
newsitem.headline: U.S.-French row holding up NATO plans to reform.

text.p: A row between France and the United States over the nationality of a high-level military commander is stopping NATO's top military officials from reforming the way the alliance works.

NATO sources said on Friday that the row -- which goes to the heart of French desires for a strong European identity in NATO -- would stop military chiefs of staff from recommending a new, leaner command structure when they meet next week.
France wants the commander of southern European forces (AFSOUTH) based in Naples, to be a European. Washington insists the job should remain, as it always has, in American hands.
"We have a blocked position," a senior military official said, expressing frustration that the row was essentially forcing NATO to take personnel decisions before it had completed its plans.

Military chiefs of staff from the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation are to meet in Brussels on November 21-22 to make recommendations to the alliance's political leaders on how NATO should work in the future.
"This will be a meeting which will not entirely be free of tension," the official said.
NATO officials had hoped that the meeting would agree to recommend a new command structure, but they said the U.S.-French row would mean no accord.

Instead, they said, German General Klaus Naumann, chairman of the NATO military committee, was likely to have to give a broad report to the North Atlantic Council on the options and views of the committee, but with no guidance.

Discussion on NATO restructuring has centred on whether to cut back on the number of regional commands, which now number three in the Atlantic and three in Europe -- AFSOUTH in Italy, AFNORTHWEST in Britain, and AFCENT in the Netherlands.

An initial idea was to cut AFNORTHWEST and create only a northern and southern command instead. The discussion, however, has come as the alliance's European countries are seeking to develop a stronger and more visible identity within NATO.

There is no question or disagreement among the countries about the nationality of the alliance's top two military officials. The supreme commanders for Europe and for the Atlantic will remain American, reflecting Washington's role as the major NATO power.
But France has made it clear that, as part of its watershed decision to return to NATO's military structure, it expects the regional commanders to be European.
The United States is said to be willing to retain all three regional commands with Europeans continuing to hold the Dutch- and British-based positions.

But it is adamant that AFSOUTH in Naples must remain under American control. The commmander in Naples is in charge of the U.S. Sixth Fleet in the Mediterranean and having a European take the post would not pass muster in the U.S. Congress.
The United States also uses the Sixth Fleet as its main "power projection" in the Middle East.
France says that there is no question of creating a situation whereby the Sixth Fleet would be commanded by anyone other than an American.

Sources said, however, they could see no immediate way out of the impasse, although they did note that the European identity in NATO was already being forged, among other things by an agreement to give the deputy supreme commander for Europe, a European, power to coordinate European actions.
